title: How Long Does It Take for Alcohol to Kick In? Timing by Drink
excerpt: Alcohol starts reaching your blood within minutes and usually peaks 30 to 90 minutes after you finish. How timing changes for shots, beer, and wine, what speeds it up, and how long it takes to wear off.
metaDescription: Most people feel a drink in 10-20 minutes, with a peak 30-90 minutes after. See timing for shots, beer, and wine, what speeds it up, and when it wears off.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how long does it take for alcohol to kick in
content:
**The quick answer:** alcohol starts to reach your blood within minutes, and most people feel the first effects within about **10 to 20 minutes** of a drink. Your blood alcohol level usually **peaks 30 to 90 minutes after you finish drinking**. On an empty stomach the peak comes early and high. After a proper meal it comes later and lower. The part that catches people out is the lag: alcohol keeps moving into your blood after you stop, so you can feel more drunk an hour from now than you do right now.

This guide walks through what happens between the first sip and the moment you feel it, how the timing changes for shots, beer, wine, and cocktails, what speeds alcohol up or slows it down, and how long it takes to wear off.

> **Safety note.** This article explains general research for adults who drink socially. It isn't medical advice, and no timing guide can tell you when you're safe to drive. If you've been drinking, don't drive. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or long gaps between breaths), has a seizure, is vomiting while passed out, or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and blood alcohol can keep rising even after someone has passed out. Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." In the US you can also call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for advice.

## How Long Does It Take for Alcohol to Kick In? The Timeline

Here's a rough timeline for one standard drink in a healthy adult. A standard drink in the US is about 14 grams of pure alcohol: a 12-ounce regular beer (around 5% alcohol), a 5-ounce glass of wine (around 12%), or a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof spirits (40%).

| Time after drinking | What's happening | What you may notice |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 5 minutes | A small amount of alcohol is absorbed through the lining of your mouth and stomach. | Usually nothing yet, apart from warmth in your throat and chest. |
| 5 to 20 minutes | Alcohol reaches the small intestine and absorption speeds up. | First effects: feeling relaxed, warmer, a little more talkative. |
| 20 to 45 minutes | Blood alcohol is rising quickly, especially on an empty stomach. | Clearer buzz, slightly slower reactions, lowered inhibitions. |
| 30 to 90 minutes | Blood alcohol reaches its peak. Faster on an empty stomach, slower after a meal. | The strongest effect from that drink. |
| After the peak | Your liver is now clearing alcohol faster than it's being absorbed. | Effects slowly fade. Some people feel tired or flat as levels drop. |

These numbers are averages. Two people drinking the same drink side by side can reach very different peaks at very different times. The rest of this article explains why.

## What Happens Between the First Sip and Feeling It

Alcohol (ethanol) is a small molecule that dissolves in both water and fat, so it passes through the lining of your gut easily. It doesn't need to be digested the way food does. That's why it acts so much faster than a meal.

### Step 1: The stomach (a small share of absorption)

A modest share of alcohol, often estimated at around a fifth, is absorbed directly through the stomach wall. The stomach also contains an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase that breaks down a little of the alcohol before it ever reaches your blood. Researchers call this **first-pass metabolism**. It's one reason the same drink produces a lower peak after you've eaten: food keeps alcohol in the stomach longer, giving that enzyme more time to work.

### Step 2: The small intestine (where most of it goes in)

Most alcohol is absorbed in the upper part of the small intestine, which has a huge surface area and a rich blood supply. Absorption there is fast. This is the single most important point about timing: **how quickly alcohol leaves your stomach for your small intestine largely decides how quickly it kicks in.** The valve between the two (the pylorus) closes when there's food to digest, which is why an empty stomach makes alcohol hit so much faster.

### Step 3: The liver gets the first look

Blood from the gut goes to the liver before it reaches the rest of your body. The liver starts breaking alcohol down immediately, first into a toxic compound called acetaldehyde and then into harmless acetate. But the liver can only process alcohol at a limited, fairly steady rate. When you drink faster than that, the excess passes through into your general circulation.

### Step 4: Your brain

Once alcohol is in your general circulation it reaches the brain within minutes. There it boosts the calming signal GABA and dampens the excitatory signal glutamate, which is why the first effects are relaxation and loosened inhibitions, followed by slower reactions, clumsiness, and slurred speech as levels rise.

### Why it keeps rising after you stop

Your blood alcohol level at any moment is a race between two things: alcohol coming in from your gut and alcohol being removed by your liver. While there's still alcohol in your stomach and intestines, it keeps flowing in. So **your blood alcohol can keep climbing for 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink**. If you judge whether you need another drink by how you feel right now, you're judging on old information. That gap is behind a lot of "I felt fine and then suddenly I didn't" nights.

## How Long Does It Take for a Shot to Kick In?

Shots tend to kick in fastest, for two reasons. First, you drink a full standard drink in a few seconds instead of over 20 minutes. Second, spirits at 40% alcohol move into the intestine and absorb quickly when you haven't eaten.

On an empty stomach, many people feel a single shot within about **10 to 15 minutes**, with the peak around **30 to 45 minutes** later. With food, both come later and the peak is lower.

The bigger issue is a round of shots. Three shots in 15 minutes means three standard drinks are all sitting in your gut, waiting to be absorbed over the next hour. You might feel moderately buzzed at the 15-minute mark and then much drunker at the 60-minute mark, without drinking anything else. If you're doing shots, the most useful rule is to space them out and wait at least 30 to 45 minutes before deciding whether you want another.

One nuance: very strong drinks (straight overproof spirits or several shots back to back) can irritate the stomach and actually slow down how fast it empties. That can make absorption a little less predictable rather than faster. It doesn't make strong drinks safer; it just makes the timing harder to judge.

## How Long Does It Take for Beer to Kick In?

Beer usually takes a bit longer to feel than a shot. A regular beer is around 5% alcohol and comes in a larger volume, and most people drink it over 15 to 30 minutes, often with food.

Typical timing for one regular beer:

- **First effects:** about 15 to 30 minutes after you start drinking
- **Peak:** roughly 45 to 90 minutes after you finish, depending on food

Watch out for craft and imported beers. Many IPAs, Belgian ales, and stouts are 7% to 10% alcohol or more, often in 16-ounce cans or pint glasses. A single pint of 8% beer is close to two standard drinks, so it can hit noticeably harder and last longer than you'd expect from "one beer." Light beers at around 4% go the other way.

## How Long Does It Take for Wine to Kick In?

A 5-ounce glass of wine at about 12% contains roughly the same alcohol as a regular beer or a shot, so the timing is similar: first effects in about **15 to 30 minutes** and a peak around **45 to 90 minutes** after you finish. Wine is often drunk with a meal, which pushes the peak later and lower.

Two things make wine stronger than it looks. Restaurant and home pours are often 6 to 9 ounces rather than 5. And many wines, especially big reds and fortified wines like port, are 14% to 20% alcohol. A generous glass of a 14.5% red can be close to two standard drinks.

Sparkling wine is a special case, which brings us to bubbles.

## Does Carbonation Make Alcohol Kick In Faster?

For many people, yes. Bubbles appear to speed up how fast the stomach empties into the intestine, which speeds absorption. A small study published in the *Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine* in 2007 gave volunteers vodka mixed with either flat or carbonated water and found that most of them reached higher blood alcohol levels faster with the carbonated version. Not everyone responded the same way, and some people showed little difference.

That fits what a lot of people notice with champagne and prosecco, and with spirits mixed with soda water or tonic. It's a reasonable rule of thumb to expect sparkling drinks to kick in a little faster than flat ones of the same strength.

## Do Diet Mixers Make You Drunker?

There's decent evidence that they can. A study by Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, compared vodka mixed with a regular sugar-sweetened soda against vodka mixed with a diet soda. The diet version produced a noticeably higher breath alcohol level, even though participants didn't feel more impaired.

The likely reason: sugar in the regular mixer is treated a bit like food. It slows how fast the stomach empties. An artificially sweetened mixer doesn't, so the alcohol moves through faster. The practical takeaway is that a "skinny" cocktail can kick in faster and peak higher than the full-sugar version, and you may not feel the difference.

## What Makes Alcohol Kick In Faster or Slower

Here's the full list of factors that change the timing, roughly in order of how much they matter.

### Food in your stomach (the biggest factor)

Eating before or while you drink is the most powerful way to slow alcohol down. Food keeps the pyloric valve closed longer, so alcohol sits in the stomach where absorption is slow and first-pass metabolism breaks some of it down. Studies over several decades have consistently found that drinking after a meal produces a lower and later peak than drinking on an empty stomach. The type of food matters less than the amount; a substantial meal with protein, fat, and fiber works better than a small snack. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) goes into more detail.

### How fast you drink

Drinking quickly front-loads your gut with alcohol, which leads to a faster, higher peak. Sipping one drink over an hour gives your liver time to keep up. This is the factor you have the most control over during the night.

### How strong the drink is

Drinks in the middle range of strength (roughly the 20% to 30% range, such as many mixed drinks) tend to be absorbed fastest. Very weak drinks like light beer absorb more slowly because the alcohol is diluted in a large volume. Very strong drinks can irritate the stomach and slow its emptying. In practice, though, the total amount of alcohol you drink matters far more than its concentration.

### Your body size and composition

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A larger person has more body water, so the same drink produces a lower concentration. Muscle holds more water than fat, so at the same weight, someone with more muscle will usually reach a lower blood alcohol than someone with more body fat.

### Sex

On average, women reach a higher blood alcohol level than men from the same amount of alcohol, even at the same body weight. Women tend to have a higher proportion of body fat and less body water, and some research suggests lower activity of the stomach enzyme that breaks down alcohol before absorption. Hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle may also play a small role.

### Medications and health conditions

Some medicines change how quickly your stomach empties or interact with alcohol in other ways. Sedating medicines (sleep aids, some antihistamines, anxiety medicines, opioid painkillers) don't necessarily make alcohol absorb faster, but they stack with its effects so you feel impaired much sooner. If you take any regular medication, ask your pharmacist how it interacts with alcohol.

People who have had certain weight-loss surgeries, especially gastric bypass, often absorb alcohol much faster and reach higher peaks, because alcohol moves almost directly into the intestine. If that applies to you, talk to your surgical team about alcohol.

### Tiredness, dehydration, and illness

Being tired doesn't change your blood alcohol much, but it makes the same level feel stronger. Fatigue and alcohol both slow your reactions and judgment, so a couple of drinks after a long week can hit like more.

### Tolerance

Tolerance changes how drunk you *feel*, not how fast alcohol gets into your blood. Someone who drinks often may feel less impaired at the same blood alcohol, but their reaction time and judgment are still affected. Tolerance is a reason to rely on counting drinks rather than on how you feel.

## How Many Drinks Does It Take to Feel It?

There's no universal number. For many average-sized adults on an empty stomach, one drink produces a mild, noticeable relaxation, and two to three drinks within an hour produces a clear buzz. Smaller people, women on average, and anyone who hasn't eaten will feel it sooner.

A more useful way to think about it is blood alcohol concentration (BAC), the percentage of your blood that is alcohol. Rough effects by BAC:

| BAC | Typical effects |
|---|---|
| 0.02% to 0.04% | Mild relaxation, warmth, slight change in mood |
| 0.05% to 0.07% | Lowered inhibitions, louder, reduced coordination and judgment |
| 0.08% | The legal driving limit in most US states. Clear impairment of reaction time, balance, and judgment |
| 0.10% to 0.15% | Slurred speech, poor coordination, slowed thinking |
| 0.16% to 0.30% | Confusion, vomiting, memory blackouts become likely |
| Above 0.30% | Risk of losing consciousness and life-threatening alcohol poisoning |

Impairment begins well below 0.08%. Driving skills are measurably affected at lower levels, which is why some countries set their limit at 0.05% or lower. Our guide to [why wine and beer can feel different](/never-hungover/wine-drunk-vs-beer-drunk) looks at how the type of drink and setting shape the experience.

## How Long Does It Take for Alcohol to Wear Off?

Getting alcohol in is fast. Getting it out is slow and steady. Your liver removes alcohol at a fairly constant rate, and on average that lowers your BAC by about **0.015 percentage points per hour**. That works out to roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, though individual rates vary.

So if you reach a BAC of 0.08% at midnight, it can take more than five hours to get back to zero. If you reach 0.15%, you may still have alcohol in your blood at breakfast.

Things that do **not** speed this up:

- Coffee (it can make you feel more alert, but your BAC is the same)
- Cold showers or fresh air
- Exercise or "sweating it out"
- Drinking lots of water (good for hydration, but it doesn't clear alcohol faster)
- Eating after you've finished drinking (food helps on the way in, not much on the way out)

The only thing that reliably lowers your BAC is time. If you want to read more about why there's no shortcut, see our guide on [whether you can speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism).

## The Lag Effect: Why "I Feel Fine" Can Be Dangerous

Because absorption takes time, there's a window where your BAC is still rising but you don't feel it yet. Three situations make this risky.

**Pre-drinking before going out.** A few fast drinks at home followed by a quick trip to the bar means you arrive just as those drinks peak, and then start drinking again.

**Drinking games and rounds of shots.** Several drinks in a short time can push BAC up for an hour or more after the game ends.

**Deciding whether to drive.** Feeling OK 20 minutes after your last drink tells you very little. Your BAC may still be climbing. Never use how you feel, or a timeline like the one in this article, to decide whether you can drive. If you've been drinking, use a ride service, public transport, or a sober driver.

The fix is simple: slow down and wait. Give each drink 30 to 60 minutes before you decide on the next one, alternate with water, and eat.

## How to Slow Alcohol Down (and Have a Better Night)

If your goal is to feel the effects more gradually and avoid getting drunker than you meant to, these habits help most:

1. **Eat a real meal before you start**, ideally with protein, fat, and fiber.
2. **Pace yourself to about one drink an hour.** That roughly matches what your liver can clear.
3. **Alternate each drink with a glass of water** or another non-alcoholic drink.
4. **Be careful with bubbles and diet mixers**, which can make alcohol kick in faster.
5. **Know what's in your glass.** Check the alcohol percentage on beer and wine, and remember that cocktails can contain two or more shots.
6. **Wait before the next round.** Give each drink time to reach its peak before you decide you need another.

These steps also tend to mean a gentler next morning. For more on that side of things, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## When to See a Doctor

For most social drinkers, the effects of alcohol are predictable and pass with time. But some situations need medical attention.

**Call 911 or get emergency help right away if someone:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and can't stay awake
- Is breathing slowly (fewer than 8 breaths a minute) or has gaps of 10 seconds or more between breaths
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting while confused or passed out
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin, or a low body temperature

While you wait for help, keep them on their side in the recovery position so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them. Don't give them coffee or a cold shower, and don't let them "sleep it off" alone.

**Talk to a doctor if you notice that:**

- Small amounts of alcohol hit you much harder or faster than they used to
- You get flushing, a racing heart, hives, or trouble breathing after drinking (this can point to alcohol intolerance or an allergy to something in the drink)
- Alcohol affects you very strongly after weight-loss surgery
- You take regular medication and aren't sure how it interacts with alcohol
- You feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or unwell when you go a day or two without drinking. That can be a sign your body has come to depend on alcohol, and it's worth a straightforward conversation with a doctor, who can help you cut back safely.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

If you're reading about how fast alcohol kicks in, it's worth being clear about what supplements can and can't do. **There is no good evidence that any supplement, including DHM, delays the effects of alcohol, keeps you sober, or lowers your BAC enough to drive.** Pacing, food, and time are what control how drunk you get.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and on the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. Some people take it before or while drinking as part of their routine for the next morning, but it isn't a way to change how alcohol kicks in. If you're curious, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly choice, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol starts entering your blood within minutes, and most people feel the first effects within about 10 to 20 minutes.
- Blood alcohol usually peaks 30 to 90 minutes after you finish drinking: sooner and higher on an empty stomach, later and lower after a meal.
- Shots hit fastest. Beer and wine are usually a little slower. Bubbles and diet mixers can speed things up.
- Your BAC can keep rising after your last drink, so wait before deciding on another.
- Alcohol leaves your body at roughly one standard drink per hour, and nothing but time speeds that up.
- Never use how you feel, or any timeline, to decide if you can drive.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long does it take for alcohol to kick in?**

Most people start to notice the first effects of a drink within about 10 to 20 minutes, because alcohol starts entering your blood within minutes of the first sip. Your blood alcohol level usually peaks somewhere between 30 and 90 minutes after you finish drinking. On an empty stomach the peak comes sooner and higher; after a full meal it comes later and lower.

**How long does it take for a shot to kick in?**

A single shot of 80-proof liquor on an empty stomach often produces noticeable effects within 10 to 15 minutes, with the peak around 30 to 45 minutes later. Because a shot is one standard drink taken all at once, it hits faster than the same amount of alcohol sipped slowly. Several shots in a row can keep pushing your blood alcohol up for an hour or more after the last one.

**How long does it take for beer or wine to kick in?**

Beer and wine usually take a little longer to feel than shots, mostly because people drink them over a longer stretch and often with food. Expect first effects within about 15 to 30 minutes and a peak roughly 45 to 90 minutes after you finish. A glass of wine and a beer contain about the same amount of alcohol per standard serving, so the drink type matters less than how fast you drink and whether you've eaten.

**Why do I feel drunk later than I expect?**

Absorption lags behind drinking. Alcohol that's still in your stomach and intestines keeps moving into your blood after you stop, so your blood alcohol can keep rising for 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink. That delay is why people who drink quickly often feel fine at first and then feel much drunker an hour later. Pausing and waiting before the next drink is the simplest way to avoid that surprise.

**Does food stop alcohol from kicking in?**

Food doesn't stop alcohol from being absorbed, but it slows it down. A meal keeps alcohol in your stomach longer, where some of it is broken down before it reaches your blood, so the peak comes later and is lower. A full meal can noticeably reduce how drunk you get from the same number of drinks. It does not make drinking a lot safe, and the alcohol still has to be cleared by your liver.

**Does carbonation make alcohol kick in faster?**

For many people it does. Carbonated drinks such as champagne or spirits mixed with soda water tend to move out of the stomach faster, which can speed absorption. Small studies have found that some people reach higher blood alcohol faster with carbonated mixers than with flat ones, though not everyone responds the same way.

**How long does it take for alcohol to wear off?**

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, lowering blood alcohol by roughly 0.015 percentage points per hour on average, or about one standard drink per hour. So the effects can last several hours after a few drinks, and much longer after a heavy night. Coffee, cold showers, and sleep don't speed this up; only time does.

**Can DHM stop alcohol from kicking in?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM blocks or delays the effects of alcohol, and it won't keep you sober or lower your blood alcohol enough to drive. DHM is studied mainly for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal research with limited human data. Pace your drinks and plan your ride home regardless of any supplement.
